papers.what_it_is: An Optics Letters preprint demonstrating single-photon-sensitive optical vibrometry by photon counting of backscattered pulses from a piezo target.

assertions.value: The authors propose and demonstrate a single-photon sensitive technique for optical vibrometry that uses high speed photon counting to sample the modulated backscattering from a vibrating target.
quotes: We propose and demonstrate a single-photon sensitive technique for optical vibrometry. It uses high speed photon counting to sample the modulated backscattering from a vibrating target.

assertions.value: The authors report that the technique detects displacements down to 110 nm and resolves vibration frequencies from DC up to several kilohertz, with less than 0.01 detected photons per pulse.
quotes: we show that this technique can detect small displacements down to 110 nm and resolve vibration frequencies from DC up to several kilohertz, with less than 0.01 detected photons per pulse

assertions.value: The authors state that interference-based vibrometry requires a laser with long coherence time and strong and stable power in the returning beam, and so cannot operate when the signal is very weak and is sensitive to intensity fluctuations from dynamic speckle patterns.
quotes: it requires a laser with long coherence time and strong and stable power in the returning beam for faithful measurement
These requirements preclude the interferencebased systems from operating when the signal is very weak
assertions.certainty_reason: Background statement about prior methods, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that speckle noise in interference-based vibrometry appears as an intensity modulation that distorts the desired phase-modulated signal, and that demodulating the two effects can be exceedingly difficult because they occur at the same frequency.
quotes: The speckle noise present in interference-based vibrometry manifests as an intensity modulation that distorts the desired phase-modulated signal.
Demodulating the two effects can be exceedingly difﬁcult because they occur at the same frequency.

assertions.value: The authors state that existing intensity-based vibrometry methods cannot operate under highly photon-starved conditions when the returning signal is single-photon level, below the sensitivity of a photodiode.
quotes: they cannot operate under highly photon-starved conditions when the returning signal is single-photon level (below the sensitivity of a photodiode)

assertions.value: The authors state that high output power can lead to eye-safety concerns, so the laser power cannot be arbitrarily increased.
quotes: High output power can lead to eye-safety concerns, meaning the laser power cannot be arbitrarily increased.

assertions.value: The authors state that time correlated single photon counting techniques using a pulsed laser synchronized to a Geiger-mode avalanche photodiode have proved successful in 3D imaging systems with less than one detected photon per pulse.
quotes: have proved successful in 3D imaging systems with less than one detected photon per pulse [14, 15]

assertions.value: The authors describe the technique as direct photon counting of the ultra-weak backscattered signal with a Geiger mode APD, using 50 MHz repetition rate pulses, with photon detections integrated over a preset dwell-time by an FPGA to form a time-series.
quotes: based on direct photon counting the ultra-weak (single-photon level) backscattered optical signal by using a Geiger mode APD

Using 50 MHz repetition rate pulses, the variation in photon counts is captured by integrating the number of photon detections over a preset dwell-time (∆t) using a ﬁeld-programmable-gate-array (FPGA).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own measurement setup in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that the digital nature of photon counting circumvents the need for a complex chain of electronic amplifiers and filters commonly found in analog detection systems.
quotes: The digital nature of photon counting circumvents the need for a complex chain of electronic ampliﬁers and ﬁlters commonly found in analog detection systems.

assertions.value: The authors state that single-photon vibrometry is fundamentally limited by the Poisson noise intrinsic to any photon counting measurement, and that the statistically random nature of the shot noise leads to unbiased baselines in both time and frequency domains, which can be mitigated through post-processing.
quotes: SPV is fundamentally limited by the Poisson noise that is intrinsic to any photon counting measurement.
the statistically random nature of such shot noise leads to unbiased baselines in both time and frequency domains, which can be mitigated through post-processing

assertions.value: The authors state that the vibration frequency can be resolved even when the signal contrast is below the shot noise by identifying the peaks in the Fourier Transformed spectrum.
quotes: The vibration frequency can be resolved even when the signal contrast is below the shot noise by identifying the peaks in the Fourier Transformed spectrum.

assertions.value: The authors report a monostatic coaxial transceiver of an angle-polished single mode fiber coupled to an aspheric lens, with a MEMS mirror for beam steering; they state the low numerical aperture of the fiber acts as a spatial filter that makes the transceiver sensitive to spatial and angular changes in the returning signal as the target moves.
quotes: The transceiver is based on a simple monostatic coaxial arrangement using off-the-shelf optical components.

The low numerical aperture of the SMF acts as a spatial ﬁlter, with a small angle of acceptance, making the transceiver sensitive to spatial and angular changes in the returning signal that occur as the target moves.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own transceiver design and detection mechanism.

assertions.value: The authors state that earlier intensity-based vibration sensors using the coupling sensitivity of single mode fiber were built for very short working distances for localized displacement sensing and do not achieve single-photon sensitivity.
quotes: but these sensors are built for very short working distances for localized displacement sensing and do not achieve single-photon sensitivity

assertions.value: The authors report that the target was a piezo-electric transducer placed 1 meter from the transceiver, with the beam fixed at a nearly normal angle of incidence and parallel to the axis of displacement.
quotes: We test the performance of SPV using a piezo-electrictransducer (PZT) placed 1 meter from the transceiver
The beam was ﬁxed at a nearly normal angle of incidence to the surface of the PZT, and parallel to the axis of displacement.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test setup and range.

assertions.value: The authors report an average outgoing power of 0.15 mW, with fiber attenuators reducing the returning signal to impose photon-starved conditions, and an InGaAs APD with detection efficiency of 10 % within a 1 ns gate, dark count rate about 50 kHz and deadtime 100 ns.
quotes: The average outgoing power was 0.15 mW
additional ﬁber attenuators were used to reduce the strength of the returning signal prior to detection, thus imposing photon-starved conditions
InGaAs APD with detection efﬁciency of 10 % within a 1 ns gate. The detector dark count rate is about 50 kHz and the deadtime is 100 ns.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own hardware parameters.

assertions.value: The authors report a mode-lock laser generating a pulse train with 6 ps full width at half maximum and 50 MHz repetition rate at 1554 nm, with a Gaussian beam diameter of 2.2 mm.
quotes: A mode-lock laser is used to generate the pulse train with 6 ps full width at half maximum (FWHM) and 50 MHz repetition rate at 1554 nm.
Collimated probe pulses (Gaussian beam diameter: 2.2 mm)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own laser parameters.

assertions.value: The authors report a fiber optics circulator that separates outgoing pulses from incoming backscattered photons with a minimum isolation ratio of 55 dB.
quotes: A ﬁber optics circulator separates the outgoing signal pulses and the incoming backscattered photons with
a minimum isolation ratio of 55 dB
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own component specification.

assertions.value: The paper defines the time varying photon count as N(t) = Phi(t) eta_det dt, where Phi(t) is the collected photon flux in photons per second and eta_det is the detector efficiency; the authors state the relation holds when the photon detection rate is much less than 1 per gate.
quotes: N(t) = Φ(t)ηdet∆t,
where Φ(t) is the collected photon ﬂux (photons/second), and ηdet is the detector efﬁciency.
Eq. (1) holds when the photon detection rate is much less than 1 per gate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition and stated regime of validity given in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that for Poisson photon counting the detection SNR is the square root of N and scales as the square root of the dwell-time, and that longer dwell-time gives better SNR at the cost of detection bandwidth, with the maximum resolvable frequency half the sampling rate.
quotes: Better SNR can be obtained with longer dwell-time, but comes at the cost of detection bandwidth (∆B = 1/2∆t).
Following the Nyquist theorem, the maximum resolvable frequency is half the sampling rate.

assertions.value: The paper defines the contrast to noise ratio as dN divided by the square root of N1 plus N2, with dN the absolute difference of two counts; the authors state that discriminating two measurements requires a CNR greater than 1.
quotes: Target displacement is detected by a differential in photon counting ∆N = |N1 − N2|, where ∆N is the sig√nal contrast.
The condition for discriminating between two m√easurements amounts to having CNR greater than 1
assertions.certainty_reason: The CNR definition and detection criterion are stated in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the square-root symbols, so the exact form is read from the surrounding words.

assertions.value: The authors report a test in which the PZT was displaced 0.55 micrometres in steps of 0.11 micrometres at an average counting rate of 275 kHz, meaning 0.0055 detections per pulse, with dwell-times of 1 ms, 10 ms and 1 second.
quotes: Figure 2 (top) shows the time-series acquired with dwell-times of 1 ms (blue), 10 ms (red), and 1 second (yellow).
In each case the PZT is displaced 0.55 µm, in steps of 0.11 µm.
The average counting rate was 275 kHz, meaning only 0.0055 detections per pulse.

assertions.value: The authors report that the counting rate changes linearly with PZT displacement, with a contrast of about 15 kHz per 0.11 micrometre step, taken from the 1 second dwell-time results.
quotes: Figure 2 (bottom) shows the linear change in the counting rate, with the contrast equal to about 15 kHz per 0.11 µm step.
The counting rates are obtained from the 1 second dwell-time results

assertions.value: The authors report a detection noise level of 22 kHz at 1 ms dwell-time with a mean counting rate of 275 kHz, about 5 kHz higher than pure shot noise, giving a CNR of 0.48 for the 1 ms data.
quotes: The detection noise level of the 1 ms dwell-time (blue) is 22 kHz, measured by taking the standard deviation of a one second segment.
Given the mean counting rate of 275 kHz, the detection noise level is about 5 kHz higher than pure shot noise
we calculate a CNR of 0.48 for the 1 ms data

assertions.value: The authors report that a dwell-time of 10 ms is sufficient to achieve CNR greater than 1 for the 110 nm displacements, confirmed by almost no overlap between signal levels in the 10 ms data of Fig. 2.
quotes: we determine a dwell-time of 10 ms is sufﬁcient to achieve CNR > 1 for the 110 nm displacements
This is conﬁrmed in Fig 2 (red) where there is almost no overlap between the signal levels at different displacements.
assertions.reader_inference: The 110 nm figure is reached at 10 ms dwell, so about 100 Hz bandwidth by the paper's own relation; the paper does not state this.

assertions.value: The paper models the photon counting time-series for a small amplitude vibration as a sine wave of amplitude A about a mean N-bar, N(t) = A sin(2 pi f t) + N-bar, where f is the target vibration frequency.
quotes: For a small amplitude vibration, the modulated photon counting time-series can be expressed as a sine wave of amplitude A oscillating about a mean value N¯
N(t) = Asin(2π f t) + N¯ ,
assertions.certainty_reason: Model stated by the paper for small amplitude vibration.

assertions.value: The authors state that the measured standard deviation combines the root-mean-square of the sine wave signal and the photon counting noise, and propose dividing the measured standard deviation by the intrinsic photon counting noise as a metric of time-domain amplitude, equal to 1 when the standard deviation is only shot noise.
quotes: The standard deviation of the measured signal σm is the sum of the root-mean-sq√uare of the sine wave signal σs and the photon counting noise N¯ .
is equal to 1 when the measured standard deviation is only from the shot noise
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the square-root symbols in Eq. (3); the paper's words say sum, though the standard combination is in quadrature.

assertions.value: The authors state that vibration frequency and amplitude information can be obtained by identifying a peak in the frequency-domain representation, obtained by applying a fast Fourier transform to the photon counting time-series.
quotes: The vibration frequency and amplitude information can be obtained by identifying a peak in the frequency-domain representation of the signal, obtained by applying fast-fourier-transform (FFT) to the photon counting time-series.

assertions.value: The authors report driving the PZT with a 150 Hz near sine wave at displacement amplitudes from 0.15 micrometres to 6.5 micrometres, with a mean detection rate about 350 kHz (0.007 detections per pulse), 1 ms dwell-time and two seconds of data.
quotes: driving the PZT with a 150 Hz near sine wave signal at displacement amplitudes ranging from 0.15 µm to 6.5 µm
The mean detection rate was ﬁxed at about 350 kHz (0.007 detection per pulse). Data was collected for two seconds with a 1 ms dwell-time.

assertions.value: The authors report that the 6.5 micrometre amplitude shows the motion in the time-domain with FFT peaks at the first three harmonics, while the 0.15 micrometre amplitude is distorted by Poisson noise in the time-domain, and its FFT still resolves the driving frequency but not the 2nd and 3rd harmonics.
quotes: Time-series of 150 Hz signal with 6.5 micron amplitude, where the contrast created is high enough that we can clearly trace the motion in the time-domain.

(b) The same setup but with 0.15 micron amplitude, where the Poisson noise distorts time-domain signal. (c) FFT of (a), showing peaks at ﬁrst three harmonics. (d) FFT of (b), still resolving driving frequency over noise, but not showing 2nd and 3rd harmonics.

assertions.value: The authors state that after the FFT the white noise is spread across the frequency domain while the signal is condensed to a narrow region, and define the peak SNR as the ratio of the FFT amplitude at the signal frequency to the standard deviation across other frequencies.
quotes: after taking the FFT, the white noise is spread across the frequency domain and the signal is condensed to a narrow region
deﬁned by the ratio between the FFT amplitude at the signal frequency and the standard deviation across other frequencies
assertions.certainty_reason: The peak SNR definition is stated by the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SNR changes linearly with amplitude in both time and frequency domains, and that the two trends are nearly identical because the total signal and noise is the same in both representations.
quotes: Figure 3 (e) shows the linear change in SNR in both frequency and time domains.
The two trends are nearly identical because the total signal and noise is the same in both representations.

assertions.value: The authors report resolving a 4 kHz vibration of 2.3 micrometre amplitude, with a dwell-time of 0.1 ms (10 kHz sampling rate) and a mean counting rate of 640 kHz.
quotes: We demonstrate the limits of the current SPV bandwidth by resolving a 4 kHz vibration, with an amplitude of 2.3 µm.
Here the dwell-time was shortened to 0.1 ms (10 kHz sampling rate), and the mean counting rate was 640 kHz.

assertions.value: The authors report that the raw FFT of a 10 second integration did not show the 4 kHz peak because of interference from the noise floor; they state that shorter dwell-time naturally leads to higher photon counting noise.
quotes: Figure 4 (a) shows the raw FFT results for a 10 second integration time.
Higher bandwidth measurements require the use of shorter dwell-time, which naturally leads to higher photon counting noise.
The signal peak cannot be identiﬁed due to the interference from the noise ﬂoor.

assertions.value: The authors state that the frequency domain noise level is inversely proportional to the square-root of the total integration time because photon counting shot noise is purely white noise.
quotes: the frequency domain noise level is inversely proportional to the square-root of the total integration time
This is because the photon counting shot noise is purely white noise.

assertions.value: The authors report that applying a 10 Hz moving-mean filter to the raw FFT of the 10 second integration resolves the 4 kHz peak, at the cost of frequency resolution, and that extending the window can oversmooth and lose signal contrast.
quotes: Figure 4 (c) shows the results when a 10 Hz moving-mean ﬁlter is applied to the raw FFT results of the 10 second integration.
Extending the windowing length of the ﬁlter can lead to oversmoothing and the loss of signal contrast altogether.

assertions.value: The authors state that diminishing improvement in peak SNR beyond a 10 Hz window length indicates the signal linewidth to be around 10 Hz.
quotes: Figure 4 (d) shows the diminishing improvement in peak SNR as the window length is extended beyond 10 Hz, which indicates the signal linewidth to be around 10 Hz.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the technique operates with less than 0.01 average detected photons per pulse, detects displacements as small as 110 nm and resolves frequencies up to 4 kHz.
quotes: Capable of operating with less than 0.01 average detected photons per pulse, the SPV technique has shown to detect vibration displacements as small as 110 nm and resolve frequencies up to 4 kHz.

assertions.value: The authors state that the measurement bandwidth can be increased using higher repetition pulses or a more efficient detector, possibly allowing single-photon sensitive vibrometry up to ultrasonic frequency; this is a proposal and was not demonstrated in the paper.
quotes: The measurement bandwidth of SPV can be increased using higher repetition pulses or a more efﬁcient detector, possibly allowing for singlephoton sensitive vibrometry up to ultrasonic frequency

assertions.value: The authors report all measurements on a PZT target at 1 meter with a near-normal beam; no rough natural target, other range or outdoor condition is reported in the text.
quotes: We test the performance of SPV using a piezo-electrictransducer (PZT) placed 1 meter from the transceiver, for precise control over the target motion.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its test target and range; the absence of other targets is the reader's reading of the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The tests used a controlled piezo target, so performance on rough remote targets is not shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that they show only a simple method of post-processing, and that the one-dimensional data offer an easily accessible platform for more extensive digital signal processing such as signal smoothing, frequency filtering and harmonic analysis.
quotes: While we only show a simple method of postprocessing in this paper, the one-dimensional data offer an easily accessible platform for more extensive digital signal processing techniques such as signal smoothing, frequency ﬁltering, and harmonic analysis.
